title: Flexible goal learning involves coordinated population activity in dCA1 and medial orbitofrontal cortex
experiments_summary:
Five adult male Long-Evans rats were implanted with 64 independently adjustable electrodes targeting dCA1 (32 electrodes) and mOFC (32 electrodes). Animals were trained on a cheeseboard maze task requiring daily learning of two new hidden reward locations across 14 recording sessions. Each session comprised three phases: pre-probe (free exploration, ~25 min), learning (40 trials divided into four 10-trial blocks), and post-probe (free exploration, ~25 min). Behavioral tracking used a DeepLabCut-based overhead video system at 50 Hz, with trajectory distance and goal-visit frequency as key metrics. Piecewise linear breakpoint analysis was applied to trial-by-trial behavioral and neural data to identify learning transitions.

Electrophysiological data were recorded at 20 kHz, processed through SpikeInterface and MountainSort4, and manually curated with phy. Units were classified into putative pyramidal cells and interneurons using CellExplorer based on spike waveform trough-to-peak latency and autocorrelogram parameters. Only units with mean firing rates ≥0.3 Hz and peak firing rates >1 Hz were retained.

Single-neuron spatial analyses used 5×5 cm binned, Gaussian-smoothed occupancy-normalized firing-rate maps (restricted to speeds >4 cm/s). Spatial information was quantified via the Skaggs information measure. Goal-related coding was assessed by computing overlap between each neuron's high-firing peak region (bins ≥80% of peak firing rate) and 3×3 bin goal windows centered on reward locations. Neurons were classified as goal-related, reorganization, or non-reorganization cells based on pre- versus post-probe firing-field alignment to previous-day versus current-day goals. A continuous peak-to-goal distance measure validated overlap-based classification. Firing-field size comparisons controlled for regional differences in field extent.

Population decoding used Gaussian Naive Bayes classifiers with leave-one-trial-out cross-validation on 400 ms non-overlapping windows of 20 ms binned firing rates, z-score normalized. Decoding was performed for behavioral-stage classification (Goal vs. Navigation, 4 classes) and learning-block classification (4 blocks), using dCA1-only, mOFC-only, and combined populations. Decoding performance was quantified as micro-average ROC-AUC. Fixed-N replacement analyses systematically substituted fractions of neurons from one region with those from the other (n=200 resamples per fraction) to test whether combined-population advantages exceeded neuron-count effects. CEBRA dimensionality reduction was applied for visualization of population state geometry.

LFP analyses used signals downsampled to 1 kHz and band-pass filtered (theta: 4–12 Hz; low gamma: 30–60 Hz; high gamma: 60–90 Hz) with 4th-order Butterworth filters. Power spectra were computed via the Welch method. Phase-locking value (PLV) measured theta-band inter-regional phase synchronization. n:m PLV quantified cross-frequency phase-phase coupling between dCA1 theta and mOFC gamma. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) was quantified as the modulation index (MI) using normalized entropy. Spike-to-theta phase locking was assessed per neuron using Rayleigh tests and von Mises distribution fitting (κ parameter). SWR events were detected from ripple-band (150–250 Hz) filtered LFP exceeding 3 SD above baseline during immobility (<4 cm/s) and excluded from LFP and spike analyses. Locomotor speed-power correlations and navigation-speed distribution comparisons between Block 1 and Block 4 were performed to rule out locomotion confounds.

Cell assemblies were detected using PCA-ICA on 20 ms binned spike data, with significant components identified by the Marchenko-Pastur threshold. Assembly activation strength was computed as a projected quadratic form, with discrete events defined as peaks exceeding a threshold of 5. SWR-contaminated periods were excluded.

Short-latency spike-time coordination was quantified via directed normalized cross-correlograms (CCGs) computed over ±50 ms at 1 ms resolution, with baseline subtraction using long-lag bins (20–50 ms). Coordination strength was taken as the maximum excess coincidence within 1–3 ms (within-region) or 1–5 ms (cross-region) windows. Significance was assessed against 1,000 jittered surrogate distributions (target spike trains shifted ±25 ms), with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q<0.05) per reference neuron. Pairs were classified as increased or decreased based on consistent linear regression slope (β) and Block 4 minus Block 1 difference (Δ) signs. Coordination changes were linked to reorganization/non-reorganization classification of constituent neurons.

A recurrent neural network (RNN) model with two subnetworks (mOFC-like reward subnetwork: 4 input units, 80 recurrent neurons; dCA1-like spatial subnetwork: 10 place-input units, 100 recurrent neurons) was implemented with short-term synaptic plasticity (STSP) using facilitating (τx=200 ms, τu=1500 ms, U=0.15) and depressing (τx=1500 ms, τu=200 ms, U=0.45) synapse parameters. The model was simulated in the RatInABox virtual environment and trained with the Adam optimizer. Three model variants were compared: full model with inter-subnetwork connectivity and STSP, same architecture without STSP, and architecture without inter-subnetwork connections. Performance was evaluated by trajectory efficiency and time-to-goal, including flexible updating after goal-location change.

Statistical analyses used nonparametric tests throughout (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman, and Dunn's post-hoc), Fisher's exact test for categorical comparisons, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction for multiple comparisons. Circular statistics used Rayleigh tests and von Mises fits. Session-level aggregation was used to reduce pseudo-replication.
